(tl;dr: my friend probably isn't cheating, but I accidentally built a machine learning model that can tell when someone plays Wordle suspiciously well.)

<p> The following was a final project for PSTAT 231, a machine learning class at UCSB. I wondered if I was sacrificing something by not making it outwardly public health-related, but I decided to follow my gut and go with something I knew I had the momentum to follow through on.</p>

<p> I later found out from my professor that they liked it so much that it'd be highlighted as an example project for future classes, so all's well that ends well? </p>


<h1> context </h1>

<p>Every day at midnight, without fail, my friend group completes the
daily Wordle, and we all post our daily summaries, listing our guesses
of the day and comparing who completed it in the least amount of
guesses.</p>
<p>And every day, by 12:15, without fail, one of my friends inevitably
gets the word in two or three.</p>
<p>He claims he’s “just lucky”.</p>
<p>I’m not sure I buy it.</p>
<p><img role="img" src="data:image/jpeg;base64," /></p>
<p>

Thus, the challenge begins: is there a way I can prove my friend is cheating using just his emoji squares?

<h1> how wordle works </h1>

- six tries to guess a five-letter English word 
- color-coded based on accuracy: green (🟩) for the right letter in the right spot, yellow (🟨) for the right letter in the wrong spot, and grey (⬛) for neither

When you finish a game of Wordle, you get a shareable emoji summary that looks like this: 

[insert here]

Despite their simplicity, there are lots of features that can be derived from these summaries, which will be instrumental to the models later on.

<h1> immediate roadblock #1 </h1>

There is no way for me to know if public Wordle games are valid or not. 

This is a problem, because a classification model needs labeled data to be trained on, so it can eventually discern from valid or invalid.  

**solution! 💡**

I decided to create my own synthetic dataset to generate labeled examples of both assisted and unassisted Wordle games.

<h1> how the engine works </h1>

At the core of the data generation process is a simulation framework that replicates the mechanics of Wordle. The engine operates on a list of valid five-letter words and enforces the same rules as the original game.

For each simulated game, a target solution word is selected, and guesses are generated sequentially. After each guess, feedback is computed using the standard Wordle rules:

Green (2): correct letter in the correct position

Yellow (1): correct letter in the wrong position

Grey (0): letter not present

The engine tracks the set of remaining candidate solutions consistent with all previous feedback. After each guess, candidate words that would produce different feedback patterns are eliminated, leaving only those still consistent with the information revealed so far.

The simulation also maintains a record of the guess history and calculates the size of the candidate set before each guess. This allows the model to approximate the entropy of the remaining search space and measure how efficiently guesses reduce uncertainty about the solution.

At the end of each simulated game, a set of summary features is extracted from the guess history, including the number of guesses taken, the rate of entropy reduction, and the fraction of green and yellow letters revealed over time.


<h1> immediate roadblock #2 </h2>

What exactly separates malicious intent from random luck?

This turned out to be an interesting thought experiment; here's what I came up with: 

- Low guess counts are suspicious, since the odds of getting the right word out of thousands of options in so few guesses are outrageously unlikely

- Random explosions of greens are suspicious, especially if there are no yellows

- Despite this, humans are imperfect, and are much more likely to make non-optimal guesses

- Along those lines, bots are much more likely to make exclusively optimal guesses that prioritize information gain

For the record, these assumptions led to some issues way down the line, but there's no point in spoiling the surprise.


In any case: the algorithms.

<h1> "Invalid" + how it works </h1>

1) start with "slate" (mathematically the best word)
2) evaluate all remaining candidate words and selects the guess that maximizes the expected entropy reduction of the candidate solution set
    - simulate the feedback pattern that each possible guess would produce against all remaining candidate solutions
    - define probability distributions over possible outcomes + compute the expected information gain
    - select the word that maximizes the expected reduction in uncertainty
3) continue until the correct word is found or the six-guess limit is reached

<h1> "Valid" + how it works </h1>

1) randomly pick a starting word
2) evaluate all remaining candidate words using a scoring function designed to mimic typical human decision-making
    - prefer guesses containing letters that have not yet been tried
    - prefer letters that appear frequently among the remaining candidate solutions
    - preserve green letters that have already been confirmed in the correct position
    - combine these components into a weighted score and select the highest-scoring candidate
3) introduce occasional imperfect play
    - with 15% probability, ignore the scoring function and select a random candidate word
    - simulates human mistakes, intuition, or suboptimal decisions
    - prevents the strategy from behaving like an information-maximizing solver
4) continue until the correct word is found or the six-guess limit is reached


Thousands of games were simulated from each strategies, which became the training data for the model.
